questions.text: Mason Durie's Te Whare Tapa Whā model represents hauora as a wharenui (meeting house) with four walls. Which statement BEST describes how the model views well-being?
options: If just one wall is strong, the wharenui will stand and the person will be well
All four walls (taha tinana, taha hinengaro, taha whānau, taha wairua) need to be strong and balanced — if one is weak, the whole structure is affected
Only the physical and mental walls really matter; the others are optional
The walls represent four separate types of people, not one person
questions.expectedAnswer: All four walls (taha tinana, taha hinengaro, taha whānau, taha wairua) need to be strong and balanced — if one is weak, the whole structure is affected
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the option about all four walls being needed and balanced.

Here's why:
Te Whare Tapa Whā models hauora as a wharenui supported by four walls — taha tinana (physical), taha hinengaro (mental/emotional), taha whānau (social/family) and taha wairua (spiritual).
If one wall is weakened, the whole structure becomes unstable, so true well-being requires all four to be looked after.
A common mistake is to think the four dimensions are independent — they are interconnected.

questions.text: A Year 10 student moved cities and lost contact with their old friends. They have started skipping kapa haka practice and feel they no longer 'belong' anywhere. Which dimension of hauora is MOST directly being affected?
options: Taha tinana — because they may be tired
Taha hinengaro — because they may feel sad
Taha whānau — because they have lost their sense of belonging and connection
Taha wairua — because they no longer believe in anything
questions.expectedAnswer: Taha whānau — because they have lost their sense of belonging and connection
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is Taha whānau.

Here's why:
Taha whānau is specifically about belonging, family, and feeling connected to wider social groups.
Losing contact with friends and stepping away from kapa haka (a group activity) is most directly a whānau dimension issue.
Note: this would also affect the other dimensions in time — that interconnection is the point of the model — but the question asks for the MOST direct dimension.

questions.text: Choose any TWO dimensions of hauora and explain how a change in one can lead to a change in the other. Use a specific Year 10 student example to support your answer (e.g. exam stress, joining a sports team, moving schools, an injury).
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for naming TWO dimensions and explaining a clear, two-way (or cause-and-effect) link between them — not just listing them.

1 mark for a specific, realistic Year 10 example that clearly shows the link in action.

Example of a strong answer: 'A Year 10 student tears their ankle and can't play netball for six weeks (taha tinana). Because netball was where they saw their friends every weekend, they start to feel isolated and left out (taha whānau). The injury directly weakened their social connections — showing how taha tinana and taha whānau are linked.'

Do not award full marks for vague answers like 'exercise makes you happy' without a specific example.

questions.text: A teenager eats a snack containing 15 g of fat, 25 g of carbohydrates, and 8 g of protein. Using the values from the chart above, calculate the total energy in the snack in kilojoules.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: From the chart: Fat = 37 kJ/g, Carbohydrates = 17 kJ/g, Protein = 17 kJ/g.

Step 2: Fat energy = 15 × 37 = 555 kJ.

Step 3: Carbohydrate energy = 25 × 17 = 425 kJ.

Step 4: Protein energy = 8 × 17 = 136 kJ.

Step 5: Total = 555 + 425 + 136 = 1116 kJ.

Step 6: Accept 1116.

questions.text: Which statement about alcohol law in New Zealand is correct?
options: There is no legal drinking age in NZ, but you must be 18 to PURCHASE alcohol from a licensed seller
You must be 21 to buy or drink alcohol in NZ
Anyone aged 16 or over can buy alcohol with a parent's note
It is legal to supply alcohol to anyone under 18 without parental consent
questions.expectedAnswer: There is no legal drinking age in NZ, but you must be 18 to PURCHASE alcohol from a licensed seller
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the first option.

Here's why:
New Zealand has no minimum legal drinking age, but the minimum PURCHASE age is 18.
It is also illegal to supply alcohol to a person under 18 without express parental consent (and even then, it must be done responsibly).
The other options are common misconceptions — there is no age 21 rule (that's the United States), parental notes do not apply, and supplying alcohol to under-18s without parental consent is an offence.

questions.text:
A Year 10 student is at a friend's place after a school sports event. Older teenagers offer them alcohol and start pressuring them to drink because 'everyone else is'.

Describe TWO different strategies the student could use to resist the pressure, and for each strategy explain WHY it would work in this scenario.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for each strategy that includes BOTH a clear action AND an explanation of why it would work in the scenario described.

Examples of strong answers:

Use a confident 'no' with a believable reason — e.g. 'No thanks, I've got training in the morning'. This works because it gives the older teens an answer they can't easily argue with and protects the student's identity as an athlete.

Leave the situation — text a parent for a ride or move to a different room/group. This works because peer pressure relies on you staying in the situation; removing yourself ends the pressure immediately and is safer than trying to argue.

Use the buddy system — have a friend agreed in advance to back each other up by both refusing. This works because it is easier to say no when you are not the only one, and reduces the social cost.

Hold a non-alcoholic drink — e.g. ask for a soft drink in a similar cup. This works because you are not 'empty-handed' and people are less likely to keep offering.

Do NOT award the second mark if the student only names a strategy without explaining WHY it would work.

options: Never feeling stressed, sad, or anxious about anything
The ability to recognise difficult emotions, use healthy coping strategies, and recover from setbacks over time
Pretending everything is fine and not telling anyone when you are struggling
Avoiding any situation that might be hard or uncomfortable
questions.expectedAnswer: The ability to recognise difficult emotions, use healthy coping strategies, and recover from setbacks over time
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the second option.

Here's why:
Resilience is NOT the absence of negative emotions — that is a common misconception.
It is the ability to feel difficult emotions, use coping strategies (talking to someone, exercise, problem-solving), and recover from setbacks.
Option 3 (hiding feelings) is actually unhealthy.
Option 4 (avoidance) tends to make things worse over time.

questions.text: Explain TWO different ways that regular physical activity can support mental well-being. For each, link it to a specific dimension of hauora and give a concrete teenager example.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for each well-explained link (way + hauora dimension + teenager example). 2 required.

Examples of strong answers:

(1) Exercise releases endorphins and lowers cortisol, improving mood (taha hinengaro). Example: 'A student who goes for a run after a hard maths test feels less stressed and more able to focus on homework.'

(2) Team sports provide a sense of belonging (taha whānau). Example: 'A Year 10 who joins a touch rugby team gains a regular group of friends, which boosts their mental well-being even on tough weeks.'

(3) Exercise improves sleep quality (taha tinana → taha hinengaro). Example: 'A teenager who plays football after school falls asleep more easily, and better sleep means better mood and concentration the next day.'

(4) Achieving a fitness goal (e.g. running 5 km) builds self-esteem and a sense of purpose (taha wairua). Example: 'Training for a school cross-country gives a student a goal to work towards, supporting their identity and self-worth.'

Do not award full marks for general statements with no example or no hauora link.

questions.text: Which statement BEST describes consent in any kind of relationship (friendship, romantic, online)?
options: Saying yes once means you've agreed for all future situations
Consent must be freely given, informed, enthusiastic, ongoing, and can be withdrawn at any time
If someone does not actively say no, they have given consent
Consent only matters in serious or romantic relationships, not friendships
questions.expectedAnswer: Consent must be freely given, informed, enthusiastic, ongoing, and can be withdrawn at any time
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the second option.

Here's why:
Consent must be: FREE (no pressure, manipulation, or coercion), INFORMED (you know what you're agreeing to), ENTHUSIASTIC (a genuine yes, not a reluctant one), ONGOING (it can be withdrawn at any time), and SPECIFIC (yes to one thing is not yes to everything).
Silence or 'not saying no' is NOT consent.
Consent applies to many situations including sharing photos, borrowing things, and physical contact — not just romantic situations.

questions.text:
A friend tells you they are being cyberbullied. Apply the Te Whare Tapa Whā hauora model to:
(a) explain how cyberbullying could affect ALL FOUR dimensions of their well-being (give a specific consequence for each dimension)
(b) describe TWO specific actions they could take, and explain which dimension of hauora each action would support most.
questions.markingGuide:
Up to 2 marks for part (a). Must address all four dimensions with a specific consequence:

Taha tinana (physical) — stress causes headaches, poor sleep, loss of appetite, lowered immunity.

Taha hinengaro (mental/emotional) — anxiety, depression, fear of checking phone, loss of self-esteem.

Taha whānau (social/family) — withdrawal from friends and family, isolation, not wanting to go to school or join group chats.

Taha wairua (spiritual) — loss of self-worth, identity, purpose; feeling hopeless about the future.

Award 1 mark for 3 dimensions explained well, 2 marks for all 4 dimensions explained well.

1 mark for part (b): TWO specific actions, each linked to the dimension it most supports. Examples:

Talk to a trusted adult (parent, teacher, school counsellor) — supports taha whānau (rebuilding connection and feeling supported) and taha hinengaro (sharing the burden).

Block and report the bully on the platform, and screenshot the messages as evidence — supports taha tinana/hinengaro (removes the constant trigger).

Contact Netsafe or 1737 — supports taha hinengaro (professional emotional support).

Do a calming physical activity (walk, sport) — supports taha tinana and taha hinengaro.

Reconnect with whānau or kapa haka — supports taha whānau and taha wairua (re-anchoring identity).

Do not award the action mark unless BOTH actions name the dimension supported and briefly justify it.
